summary: Phú Yên is a south-central coastal province known for the country's largest ocean tuna fishery (Vũng Rô, Đông Tác) and for brackish lagoons such as Ô Loan and Cù Mông that yield distinctive seafood. Phú Yên cooking leans clean and lightly spiced, making the most of live sea produce — above all ocean tuna eye, Ô Loan blood cockles and bánh canh hẹ.

mat-ca-ngu-dai-duong.description: Mắt cá ngừ đại dương (ocean tuna eye) is bound up with the tuna-line fishery of the Phú Yên fishermen, whose catch is the largest in the country. Each tuna weighing tens of kilos yields only a single pair of eyes the size of a fist, rich and nutty in taste and regarded as the finest and most nourishing part of the fish, which has made it a rare and costly speciality.
keyIngredients: Thuốc bắc (Chinese herbal tonic ingredients: jujube, goji berry, lotus seed)
prepOutline: Clean the tuna eyes, rub them with ginger wine to take off the fishiness, then wash off the slime
Arrange the eyes in a lidded pot with thuốc bắc (Chinese herbal tonic ingredients: jujube, goji berry, lotus seed), ginger and seasoning
Double-boil for several hours over a low flame until the eyes are soft and the broth clean and sweet
Adjust the seasoning and scatter over spring onion and pepper before serving
mat-ca-ngu-dai-duong.howToEat: Eat it hot, straight from the pot, each portion ladled into its own small bowl as a tiềm (double-boiled tonic), with bread or plain rice alongside, and drink down the rich, sweet broth the eye releases.

banh-canh-he.description: Bánh canh hẹ is a common breakfast right across Phú Yên, set apart from bánh canh (thick rice-flour noodles) elsewhere by the sharp bite of finely chopped fresh garlic chives strewn over the top. The broth is simmered from bones and fresh fish — usually mackerel or sailfish — the noodles are soft and springy rice flour, and it is eaten with both fried and steamed chả cá (fish cake).
keyIngredients: Bones and fish for the broth
prepOutline: Simmer the broth from pork bones and fish heads for several hours until it is sweet and clear
Boil the fresh rice-flour bánh canh (thick noodles) until just done
Fry some of the chả cá (fish cake) golden and steam the rest so it stays soft and springy
Blanch the noodles, ladle over the hot broth, arrange the chả cá on top and scatter with chopped garlic chives
banh-canh-he.howToEat: Eat it hot the moment it is ladled into the bowl, with a squeeze of lime and ground or fresh chilli to lift it, stirring the garlic chives through the broth before you drink it.

so-huyet-dam-o-loan.description: Ô Loan lagoon, in Tuy An district, is a well-known stretch of brackish water in Phú Yên that produces blood cockles with thick, sweet, richly flavoured flesh thanks to its particular ecology. Ô Loan blood cockles were granted a geographical indication certificate by the Intellectual Property Office in 2018, confirming their standing as a regional speciality.
prepOutline: Soak the cockles in rice-washing water with chilli so they spit out the sand
Steam or briefly boil them with bruised sả (lemongrass) until the shells just open
They can also be grilled over than hoa (charcoal) with spring onion oil to bring up the aroma
Prepare a salt, pepper and lime dip, or mắm gừng (nước mắm, Vietnamese fish sauce, with ginger), to go with them
so-huyet-dam-o-loan.howToEat: Eat them while still hot, prising the shells apart by hand and dipping in salt, pepper and lime or in mắm gừng (nước mắm, Vietnamese fish sauce, with ginger); they are usually served as a dish with drinks, with rau răm (Vietnamese coriander) alongside.
